{"content": "1|# Spring Boot Masterclass
2|### Real-Time Messaging Platform — Teaching Session Notes
3|
4|---
5|
6|## 1. What Is Spring Boot?
7|
8|**Spring** (2003) — Powerful Java framework but required massive XML configuration files. Hundreds of lines of config before writing a single line of business logic.
9|
10|**Spring Boot** (2014) — Solved this with one philosophy:
11|
12|> **"Convention over Configuration"** — Sensible defaults. You only configure what you *want to change.*
13|
14|Spring Boot is **not a separate framework**. It is Spring with:
15|
16|| Feature | What it does |
17||---|---|
18|| Auto-configuration | Reads your dependencies and configures itself automatically |
19|| Embedded server | Server runs *inside* your JAR. No external Tomcat needed. |
20|| Starter dependencies | One line pulls in everything (e.g. `spring-boot-starter-web`) |
21|| Production-ready tools | Health checks, metrics, etc. out of the box |
22|
23|---
24|
25|## 2. The IoC Container & Dependency Injection
26|
27|Spring's core idea: **Inversion of Control (IoC)**.
28|
29|**Normal Java (you control everything):**
30|```java
31|UserService userService = new UserService();
32|UserRepository repo = new UserRepository();
33|userService.setRepository(repo); // YOU wire it manually
34|```
35|
36|**Spring's way (Spring controls it):**
37|```java
38|@Service
39|public class UserService {
40|    @Autowired
41|    private UserRepository repo; // Spring creates and injects this
42|}
43|```
44|
45|You **declare what you need**. Spring **creates and injects** it.
46|This is called **Dependency Injection (DI)**.
47|
48|> Think of Spring as a **factory manager**. You put up signs saying what you need, and the factory delivers it.
49|
50|---
51|
52|## 3. Layered Architecture
53|
54|The standard Spring Boot architecture:
55|
56|```
57|HTTP Request
58|     ↓
59|┌─────────────┐
60|│  Controller │  ← Handles incoming API requests, returns responses
61|└──────┬──────┘
62|       ↓
63|┌─────────────┐
64|│   Service   │  ← Contains the actual business logic / processing
65|└──────┬──────┘
66|       ↓
67|┌─────────────┐
68|│ Repository  │  ← Database operations as Java methods (no raw SQL)
69|└──────┬──────┘
70|       ↓
71|┌─────────────┐
72|│  Database   │  ← PostgreSQL
73|└─────────────┘
74|```
75|
76|### Why separate Controller and Service?
77|- **Controller** = traffic cop. Receives request, calls service, returns response. Nothing more.
78|- **Service** = the brain. Validation, business rules, orchestration.
79|- Keeps code clean, testable, and maintainable.
80|
81|---
82|
83|## 4. Entity vs DTO
84|
85|### Entity
86|- Represents a **row in the database**
87|- Mapped directly to a table via Hibernate
88|- Contains ALL fields including sensitive ones
89|
90|```java
91|@Entity
92|@Table(name = "users")
93|public class User {
94|    private Long id;
95|    private String username;
96|    private String password;  // BCrypt hashed — NEVER send this to client
97|    private boolean online;
98|}
99|```
100|
101|### DTO (Data Transfer Object)
102|- A **clean, controlled contract** with the outside world
103|- Contains only what the client needs to see
104|- Used for both **request bodies** (coming in) and **response bodies** (going out)
105|
106|```java
107|// Response DTO — safe to send to client
108|public class UserResponse {
109|    private Long id;
110|    private String username;
111|    private boolean online;
112|    // NO password field
113|}
114|```
115|
116|### Why both?
117|> If you return the Entity directly → you expose the hashed password, internal IDs, audit fields — your entire database structure. The DTO is a protective filter between your DB and the outside world.
118|
119|**Rule:** Entity ↔ DB. DTO ↔ Client. Never mix them.
120|
121|---
122|
123|## 5. Repository & Hibernate (ORM)
124|
125|### The Problem
126|Java deals in **objects**. PostgreSQL deals in **tables and rows**. Someone has to translate between the two worlds.
127|
128|### Hibernate — The ORM
129|**ORM = Object Relational Mapper**. Maps Java objects ↔ database rows automatically.
130|
131|```
132|Java Object (User)        Hibernate              PostgreSQL (users table)
133|──────────────────   ──────────────────────   ──────────────────────────
134|user.id          →   INSERT INTO users     →   id = 1
135|user.username    →   (id, username, pwd)   →   username = 'luffy'
136|user.password    →   VALUES (...)          →   password = '$2a...'
137|```
138|
139|You write **zero SQL**. Hibernate writes it for you.
140|
141|### JpaRepository
142|Spring Data JPA gives you `JpaRepository` — an interface with built-in methods:
143|
144|```java
145|public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
146|    Optional<User> findByUsername(String username); // Spring writes the SQL
147|}
148|```
149|
150|**Full picture:**
151|```
152|Your Code (Repository interface)
153|        ↓
154|   Spring Data JPA
155|        ↓
156|     Hibernate (writes & executes SQL)
157|        ↓
158|    PostgreSQL
159|```
160|
161|---
162|
163|## 6. WebSocket
164|
165|### REST vs WebSocket
166|
167|```
168|REST (Half-duplex / Request-Response):
169|Client ──── request ────→ Server
170|Client ←─── response ─── Server
171|Server can NEVER speak first. Ever.
172|
173|WebSocket (Full-duplex / Persistent):
174|Client ←──────────────→ Server
175|Both can send messages anytime. Simultaneously.
176|```
177|
178|### Why WebSocket for chat?
179|The server needs to **push** a new message to you the moment it arrives — without you asking for it. REST cannot do this. WebSocket can.
180|
181|### The Handshake (3 steps)
182|```
183|Step 1 — Client sends HTTP Upgrade request:
184|   GET /ws HTTP/1.1
185|   Upgrade: websocket
186|
187|Step 2 — Server accepts, sends 101:
188|   HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
189|   Upgrade: websocket
190|
191|Step 3 — Protocol upgrades to WebSocket:
192|   Persistent, full-duplex TCP connection established.
193|   Both sides can now send messages freely.
194|```
195|
196|### Our Project's Two Channels
197|```
198|Frontend ←── REST API ───→ Backend     (login, register, message history)
199|Frontend ←── WebSocket ──→ Backend     (real-time messages, status updates, presence)
200|```
201|
202|---
203|
204|## 7. JWT (JSON Web Token)
205|
206|### The Movie Ticket Analogy
207|When you buy a movie ticket:
208|- It has your name, seat, movie, date
209|- It has a **stamp/signature** from the theatre — nobody can fake it
210|- At the door they check the stamp — they **don't call a database**
211|
212|**JWT is that ticket.**
213|
214|### Structure
215|```
216|xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz
217|  ↑      ↑      ↑
218|Header  Payload  Signature
219|```
220|
221|| Part | Contains |
222||---|---|
223|| Header | Algorithm used to sign (e.g. HS256) |
224|| Payload | Actual data: `userId`, `username`, `expiry time` |
225|| Signature | Secret stamp — proves it wasn't tampered with |
226|
227|### Login Flow
228|```
229|1. Frontend sends { username, password }
230|2. Backend verifies password with BCrypt
231|3. Backend creates JWT → { userId: 1, username: "luffy", exp: 1hr }
232|4. Backend signs it with a SECRET KEY only the server knows
233|5. Sends token back to frontend
234|6. Frontend stores token, sends it in every future request
235|```
236|
237|### Every Future Request
238|```
239|1. Frontend sends → "Authorization: Bearer ***
240|2. Backend reads the token
241|3. Verifies signature using its SECRET KEY
242|4. If valid → extracts userId → proceeds
243|5. No database lookup needed. Ever.
244|```
245|
246|> This is **stateless authentication** — the server remembers nothing. The token carries everything.
247|
248|### What if the token is stolen?
249|**The server will accept a stolen token.** It's genuine — the signature is valid. The server cannot know it was stolen.
250|
251|**The defenses:**
252|
253|| Defense | How it helps |
254||---|---|
255|| Short expiry (e.g. 1 hour) | Stolen token becomes useless quickly |
256|| HTTPS only | Token is encrypted in transit — hard to steal |
257|| Logout blacklist | Server tracks invalidated tokens (breaks statelessness) |
258|
259|> This is why the requirements say **"short-lived session tokens"** — it's the primary defense.
260|
261|---
262|
263|## 8. Token Storage on the Client
264|
265|The browser gives you 3 options:
266|
267|| Storage | JS Access | Survives Refresh | Survives Tab Close | Security |
268||---|---|---|---|---|
269|| `localStorage` | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ❌ Vulnerable to XSS |
270|| `sessionStorage` | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | ❌ No | ❌ Vulnerable to XSS |
271|| HTTP-only Cookie | ❌ No | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ✅ Most secure |
272|
273|### Why HTTP-only Cookie wins
274|- **localStorage/sessionStorage**: Any JavaScript on the page can read them. If an attacker injects malicious JS (XSS attack) they simply run `localStorage.getItem('token')` → token stolen.
275|- **HTTP-only Cookie**: JavaScript **cannot access it at all** — not even your own code. Browser sends it automatically with every request. XSS attack? The malicious JS can't touch the cookie.
276|
277|> Our project will use **HTTP-only cookies** to store the JWT.
278|
279|---
280|
281|## 9. Planned Backend Project Structure
282|
283|```
284|backend/
285|├── auth/
286|│   ├── AuthController.java        ← POST /api/auth/login, /register, /logout
287|│   ├── AuthService.java           ← BCrypt verify, JWT issue
288|│   ├── AuthRepository.java        ← Find user by username
289|│   └── dto/
290|│       ├── LoginRequest.java
291|│       ├── RegisterRequest.java
292|│       └── AuthResponse.java
293|│
294|├── user/
295|│   ├── UserController.java        ← GET /api/users
296|│   ├── UserService.java           ← Get all users, online status
297|│   ├── UserRepository.java
298|│   └── dto/
299|│       └── UserResponse.java      ← id, username, online (NO password)
300|│
301|├── chat/
302|│   ├── ChatController.java        ← GET /api/messages/{otherUserId}
303|│   ├── ChatService.java           ← Save, fetch, update message status
304|│   ├── MessageRepository.java
305|│   └── dto/
306|│       ├── SendMessageRequest.java
307|│       └── MessageResponse.java
308|│
309|├── websocket/
310|│   ├── WebSocketHandler.java      ← Handles WS events (send, read, presence)
311|│   └── WebSocketConfig.java       ← WS endpoint config + authentication
312|│
313|└── entity/
314|    ├── User.java                  ← Shared by auth + user + chat
315|    └── Message.java               ← Shared by chat + websocket
316|```
317|
318|### Why is `entity/` a separate top-level folder?
319|`User.java` is needed by **Auth** (login), **User** (profile/list), and **Chat** (who sent the message).  
320|`Message.java` is needed by **Chat** (REST history) and **WebSocket** (real-time delivery).
321|
322|If you put `User.java` inside `auth/`, then `chat/` and `user/` would have to import from `auth/` — creating **tight coupling** between modules. Bad design.
323|
324|Entities are **shared database objects**. They belong to no single module. They live at the root.
325|
326|---
327|
328|## 10. REST API Contracts (Frontend ↔ Backend)
329|
330|```
331|POST   /api/auth/register      { username, password }     → { user, token }
332|POST   /api/auth/login         { username, password }     → { user, token }
333|POST   /api/auth/logout                                   → 200 OK
334|GET    /api/users                                         → [ { id, username, online } ]
335|GET    /api/messages/{userId}                             → [ { id, text, senderId, recipientId, timestamp, status } ]
336|```
337|
338|---
339|
340|## 11. WebSocket Event Schema
341|
342|```
343|Client → Server:
344|  SEND_MESSAGE    { text, recipientId }
345|  MESSAGE_READ    { messageId }
346|
347|Server → Client:
348|  NEW_MESSAGE     { id, text, senderId, recipientId, timestamp, status: 'delivered' }
349|  STATUS_UPDATE   { messageId, status: 'delivered' | 'read' }
350|  PRESENCE_UPDATE { userId, online: true | false }
351|```
352|
353|---
354|
355|## 12. Message Delivery States (3-State System)
356|
357|```
358|Message sent by user
359|        ↓
360|  [PENDING]   ← Server received & persisted to DB
361|        ↓
362|  [DELIVERED] ← Recipient client received it via WebSocket
363|        ↓
364|  [READ]      ← Recipient opened/viewed the message
365|```
366|
367|All 3 state transitions are **pushed to the sender in real time via WebSocket**.
368|
369|---
370|
371|## Key Principles Learned
372|
373|> **1.** Never return Entities directly — always use DTOs  
374|> **2.** JWT is stateless — the token IS the session  
375|> **3.** Short-lived tokens are the primary defense against theft  
376|> **4.** HTTP-only cookies protect against XSS — localStorage does not  
377|> **5.** WebSocket for push, REST for pull  
378|> **6.** Entities are shared — they belong at the root, not inside a module  
379|> **7.** Hibernate writes the SQL — you write Java  
380|> **8.** Persist first, deliver second — guarantees zero message loss
